title: AI-Assisted Single-Cell Analysis with R
text:
Choose your starting point
Start with synthetic practice, repeat the workflow with published mouse-brain data, then bring your own study.
This first practical covers cell quality control (QC), counts per 10,000, log transformation and principal component analysis (PCA). It does not assign new cell types or test treatment effects. Cells from one donor are not independent biological replicates.
Human → AI → Human: decide the question yourself; ask AI to explain a command or critique a claim; check its answer against your files and calculations. Never accept a biological claim solely because AI generated it.
Begin with setup, then follow synthetic practice. The same commands and file conventions apply to the real example and your own study.
Complete the paths in this order on your first visit. A later return can begin at the relevant step, but changing inputs or cutoffs means rerunning checks, analysis and verification.
Your main deliverable is not just a plot. It is a short report in which a reader can trace a claim to its input, method, saved output and check. You will learn the same habits with simulated counts before applying them to a real study.

title: Set up the project
text:
1. Download and open the complete project
Open the GitHub repository, select Code → Download ZIP, then extract the ZIP.
In VS Code, choose File → Open Folder and select the extracted project folder. A GitHub ZIP usually names it ai-assisted-single-cell-analysis-main. Open the inner folder if there is an extra outer folder. Do not work inside the compressed ZIP.
Check that you can see _quarto.yml, renv.lock, data/, scripts/ and examples/ directly inside the selected folder. The complete project also includes .Rprofile and renv/activate.R. These may be hidden in your file browser.
Choose Terminal → New Terminal. This is the main project folder. Run guide commands here unless the instructions explicitly say to enter reports/.

title: Set up the project
text:
Terminal or R console?



Commands beginning with Rscript or quarto go in the terminal. The > prompt means you are inside R; exit with q(save = "no") before using terminal commands. Copy commands without any displayed prompt symbols. Ctrl+Z suspends R; it does not exit R.

title: Set up the project
text:
2. Check the tools
Install R and Quarto. RStudio is optional. The worked examples were checked on macOS with R 4.6.1. Use the R version recorded in the supplied renv.lock; renv restores packages but does not install R itself.
In the terminal:
Rscript --version
quarto --version
Both should print a version. If either command is not found, finish installing that tool and reopen the terminal.

title: Set up the project
text:
3. Restore the analysis environment
Rscript scripts/R/setup.R
An internet connection is required on the first run. Wait for Setup complete. The script restores the package versions in renv.lock, checks that required packages load and confirms that the project is synchronized. It does not create a new lockfile or update packages to current releases.
If setup fails, stop before running analysis and use installation troubleshooting. A missing lockfile means the download is incomplete or the maintainer has not supplied the tested environment.

title: Set up the project
text:
4. Start the synthetic practice
Open Define: Synthetic practice, then follow its seven steps in order. The commands you will use are:
Rscript scripts/R/prepare_synthetic.R
Rscript scripts/R/check_inputs.R synthetic
Rscript scripts/R/run_workflow.R synthetic
Rscript scripts/R/verify_cell.R synthetic Cell001
Rscript scripts/R/verify_cell.R synthetic Cell047
Rscript scripts/R/verify_cell.R synthetic Cell048
Run one line at a time. Stop if a command fails. Expected: 1,000 genes, 200 cells, 190 retained, followed by three PASS messages. Cell047 and Cell048 should have retained FALSE; the verifier passes because it confirms their exclusion.

title: Set up the project
text:
5. Preview the guide
quarto preview
The book explains commands without running analysis during rendering. Figures come from the R workflow. Stop the preview with Ctrl+C when you need the terminal again.
After synthetic practice, follow the Zeisel example. Use your own study only after you understand the inputs and verification. Report-writing instructions are in Write the report.

title: One workflow for every dataset
text:
Find your outputs
Follow each example from Define to Write. Use synthetic, zeisel or your-study consistently as the dataset name. Read the page before copying its command.
DATASET means the dataset name; replace it with synthetic, zeisel or your-study. All folders are created automatically by the workflow.
Run commands one at a time. Continue only after success. Recreate inputs only when needed; after changing inputs or QC cutoffs, rerun Check, Run and Verify before interpreting results. The verifier detects changed input bytes. A successful command checks calculation, not scientific interpretation.
Keep learner-generated reports in the ignored reports/ folder. Write the report explains how to create one without adding it to the book.

title: One workflow for every dataset
section: Three habits to carry through every example
text:
Three habits to carry through every example
Keep decisions separate from calculations. The script applies your cutoffs; you justify them. It calculates PCA; you decide what the design and metadata allow you to say about it.
Keep inputs, results and writing distinct. Raw files belong in data/DATASET/, generated outputs in results/DATASET/ and learner writing in reports/. A report should identify the run it describes. Rerunning the script does not rewrite your report’s prose.
Use AI at a specific point. First make your own prediction or observation. Then ask AI to explain a command or question a claim using supplied evidence. Finally compare its response with the actual files and revise your own explanation. Share only data you are permitted to disclose; do not send participant identifiers.
At each step, keep a brief note of what you did, what you observed and what remains uncertain. Those notes become the Methods, Results and Limitations sections of the report.

title: Write the report
text:
1. Create the starter
A short report explains the question, checked results and limitations in your own words. Use AI to review clarity, then compare every claim with your saved outputs.
From the main project folder:
For the real example, use zeisel; for your study, use your-study. The command creates reports/synthetic-report.qmd and a local Quarto configuration. It keeps an existing report rather than overwriting it. Starter text is stored in templates/report.qmd; learner writing belongs in reports/.

title: Write the report
text: Rscript scripts/R/create_report.R synthetic

title: Write the report
text:
2. Edit your report
Open the new QMD in VS Code or RStudio. Replace every bracketed instruction with your own text. Include:

The question, source and study design.
Input checks, thresholds and retained-cell count.
One QC observation and one PCA observation, with saved values.
A manually checked cell calculation and its verifier result.
What remains uncertain and one justified next step.
How AI was used and how you checked its response.

Figures are already linked to results/DATASET/figures/. Supporting tables are in results/DATASET/tables/. Revisit your interpretation whenever inputs or cutoffs change. Previously written reports do not update their prose automatically.

title: Write the report
text:
3. Render and read
After running the analysis, enter reports/ and render:
cd reports
quarto render synthetic-report.qmd
cd ..
Replace the report filename when using another dataset. The HTML stays in reports/; its figures are embedded for convenient sharing. Confirm that both display and that no bracketed starter text remains. Inspect the report for private metadata before sharing.
The complete reports/ folder is ignored by Git. Do not add reports to _quarto.yml or commit learner writing. The book’s seven-step examples remain separate from these reports.

text:
Make each claim traceable

tables/selected-genes.tsv


Which files and software were used

The table paths above are inside results/DATASET/. State rounded values in the report, but compare full values during verification. A verification record can be compact: cell ID, quantity/gene, manual value, saved value and verdict.
An observation describes what the output shows. An interpretation proposes what it means. A limitation explains why that meaning is not established or how far it can be generalized. Keep all three visible. Neither a successful script nor AI approval replaces a scientific argument.
Before sharing, read the rendered report as though you had not run the code: can you identify the question, reconstruct the key check and understand the strongest supported conclusion without guessing?

title: Define: Synthetic practice
text:
The question
After basic cell quality checks, are the two simulated expression populations distinguishable in an exploratory PCA?
Begin with data whose construction is known. You can check whether the workflow produces the intended outputs before applying it to a study with unknown biology.
The practice dataset has 1,000 genes and 200 cells. Two populations, Simulated A and Simulated B, have different expected expression for selected genes. Cells also vary in total counts and expression within each population. Five cells have deliberately low counts; five have deliberately high mitochondrial fractions.
These are simulated gene counts, not measurements from an organism. The four Practice sample IDs are bookkeeping labels, not real donors or biological replicates. The simulation is not fitted to the Zeisel dataset.

title: Define: Synthetic practice
text:
What you will learn
You will trace a cell through the count matrix, check its metadata, examine QC decisions, interpret PCA and independently recalculate one result. The final output is a short report that explains both an observation and its limits.
The analysis can show whether the constructed patterns remain visible after this QC and normalization. It cannot discover a new biological cell type, establish a treatment effect or demonstrate how a real tissue behaves.

title: Define: Synthetic practice
text:
Your task
Before running anything, write two sentences:

“My question is …”
“Even if the PCA separates the populations, I cannot conclude …”

Then predict how a low-count cell might affect a normalized value. You will revisit this after checking Cell047.
Optional AI prompt: “Critique the scope of my question about simulated single-cell counts. Separate a calculation I can verify from a biological claim these data cannot support.”
Before moving on: you should be able to explain why known simulation labels help evaluate a workflow without constituting biological evidence.

title: Preview: Synthetic practice
text:
Know what you are working toward
You will create a QC table, two figures and a report. Read this page first so the outputs have a purpose; return after Run to inspect your own figures.
Supporting files record cutoffs, input checksums, selected genes and software versions. One workflow for every dataset lists all locations.

title: Preview: Synthetic practice
text:
Output
What it helps you answer




results/synthetic/tables/cell-qc.tsv
Which cells pass the stated QC rules?


results/synthetic/figures/qc.png
How do count depth, detected genes and mitochondrial fractions vary?


results/synthetic/figures/pca.png
What expression patterns are visible among retained cells?


results/synthetic/tables/pca-variance.tsv
How much selected-gene variation does each component capture?

title: Preview: Synthetic practice
text:
Read the QC panels



Synthetic cell QC: depth, detected genes and mitochondrial fraction.


The left panel compares total counts with detected genes. The right compares total counts with mitochondrial percentage. Blue means retained; red means excluded by at least one cutoff. Dashed lines show the cutoffs.
In the checked run, 190 of 200 cells are retained. Low-depth cells appear near the lower-left of the first panel. The deliberately high-mitochondrial cells can have hundreds of detected genes yet still fail the mitochondrial cutoff. No single panel explains every exclusion.

title: Preview: Synthetic practice
text:
Read the PCA



PCA of retained synthetic cells, coloured by known simulation labels.


Each point is one retained cell. PC1 and PC2 are weighted combinations of selected, transformed gene expression. Cells close together on these two axes have similar scores in this projection; they may still differ along other components.
The known simulated populations separate mainly along PC1, with variation within each population. In the checked run, PC1 explains about 5.5% and PC2 about 1.6% of variance in the selected transformed genes. Most variation is outside this plot. Colours display construction labels; the algorithm did not infer cell types.

title: Preview: Synthetic practice
text:
Your task
Point to the axis and metric relevant to each statement: “few detected genes,” “high mitochondrial fraction” and “separated PCA scores.” Write one observation without using “significant” or naming a biological cell type.
Before moving on: distinguish an output you expect to create from a result you have actually generated and checked. Missing figures before Run mean that the workflow has not generated them yet.

title: Meet: Synthetic practice
text:
Prepare the inputs
From the main project folder, run:
This recreates the practice inputs using seed 20261125 and explicitly selected R random-number settings. It overwrites synthetic TSV inputs; it does not prepare the real dataset or your personal study. If data/synthetic/counts.rds exists, move it aside first: the reader gives RDS priority, and the generator stops to avoid competing inputs.

title: Meet: Synthetic practice
text: Rscript scripts/R/prepare_synthetic.R

title: Meet: Synthetic practice
text:
Understand the three tables








File in data/synthetic/
Rows
Meaning




counts.tsv
1,000 genes
gene_id, followed by 200 cell columns


cell-metadata.tsv
200 cells
cell_id, sample_id, reference_label, simulation_note


gene-metadata.tsv
1,000 genes
gene_id, is_mito



A count-matrix entry is a simulated nonnegative integer. A zero is an observed zero count in the simulation; it is not a missing value. NA would mean unavailable data and is rejected by this workflow.
Cells are columns, genes are rows. Cell001 therefore names a column in the count matrix and one row in the cell metadata. Do not transpose the matrix to make it resemble the metadata.

title: Meet: Synthetic practice
text:
Understand what was constructed
Genes 1–20 are flagged mitochondrial. Genes 21–100 have increased expected expression in A; genes 101–180 have increased expected expression in B. Random count variation, unequal depths and cell-specific expression variation make individual profiles different. The simulation uses negative-binomial draws for ordinary cells, allowing more variability than a fixed profile copied across cells.
reference_label and simulation_note describe construction settings. QC decisions use counts and mitochondrial flags, not those labels. Known populations colour the PCA only after its scores have been calculated. provenance.txt records the construction and R version.

title: Meet: Synthetic practice
text:
Your task
Open each TSV in VS Code. Find Cell001 in the matrix and metadata. Find Gene001 in the gene table and confirm that is_mito is TRUE. Identify one cell marked low depth and one marked high mitochondrial fraction.
Explain the difference between sample_id and reference_label: one identifies an artificial source label, the other a simulated expression population. Neither supplies measured donor replication.
Before moving on: you can trace a count to the correct cell and gene without relying on row order alone.

title: Check: Synthetic practice
text:
Validate the files
Expected output includes 1,000 genes, 200 cells and four sample ID values, followed by an identifier/raw-count check success message.
The checker rejects missing or duplicate identifiers, mismatched metadata IDs, nonnumeric values, negative or fractional counts and missing counts. It checks required metadata columns and logical mitochondrial flags. When IDs match but appear in different orders, it aligns metadata to matrix order.
A successful check means the files meet this script’s input contract. It does not establish biological replication, meaningful labels or appropriate thresholds.

title: Check: Synthetic practice
text: Rscript scripts/R/check_inputs.R synthetic

title: Check: Synthetic practice
text:
Review the QC rules
Open config/qc.tsv. The synthetic row should contain:








Rule
Value
A cell passes when…




min_counts
500
Total counts are at least 500


min_genes
200
At least 200 genes have positive counts


max_mito_pct
30
Mitochondrial counts are at most 30% of total counts



A cell must pass all three and have a positive total. A zero-total cell is excluded; its mitochondrial percentage is undefined (NA). The parameters are recorded during Run.
These cutoffs were chosen for this teaching dataset. They are not a recommendation for every organism, technology or tissue. A high mitochondrial fraction may motivate investigation; the flag alone does not prove that a real cell is damaged.

title: Check: Synthetic practice
text:
Predict two decisions
Cell047 was deliberately generated with only 85 total counts. Even before plotting, you can predict that it fails the minimum-count rule. Cell048 has adequate counts but a deliberately high mitochondrial fraction; check the right QC panel before explaining its exclusion.

title: Check: Synthetic practice
text:
Your task
Record the matrix dimensions and the three cutoffs. State which checks are automated and which depend on understanding the study. If a check fails, correct the input or investigate the cause; do not bypass it simply to produce a plot.
Optional AI prompt: “Explain these three QC rules in plain language. Ask what evidence I should inspect before transferring them to another dataset.”
Before moving on: the input check passes and you understand the retention rule you are about to apply.

title: Run: Synthetic practice
text:
Run once, then inspect
Expected summary: 190 of 200 cells retained. Messages saying null device followed by 1 are normal: R has finished writing a figure.
Start with results/synthetic/tables/cell-qc.tsv. It includes every input cell, the three QC metrics and retained. Excluded cells remain in this table but do not enter normalization or PCA.

title: Run: Synthetic practice
text: Rscript scripts/R/run_workflow.R synthetic

title: Run: Synthetic practice
text:
What the script calculates
For a retained cell, let (T) be its total raw counts and (x_g) a gene’s count. The saved transformed value is:
[ y_g=(1+10{,}000). ]
Dividing by the cell total adjusts each cell to a common total of 10,000 before transformation. log is the natural logarithm; log1p(z) calculates log(1 + z). The saved log-transformed values no longer sum to 10,000. This simple scaling does not remove every technical effect or justify treatment comparisons.
The script computes gene variance across retained cells, selects up to 500 genes with positive variance, and runs PCA after centering genes. It does not scale genes to unit variance. It does not remove mitochondrial genes from feature selection, so technical or QC-related variation can remain important.
Population labels do not enter normalization, feature selection or PCA. They are used to colour synthetic points after scores are calculated.

All paths in the table are inside results/synthetic/. The workflow records input checksums and session information as well.

title: Run: Synthetic practice

Your task
Record 200 input cells, 190 retained cells and 10 exclusions. Return to Preview and describe the two figures using your generated outputs. If the numbers differ, confirm the seed, input version and cutoffs before writing an interpretation.
Before moving on: the figures exist, their source tables are identifiable, and you are ready to verify a calculation independently.

title: Verify and Explain: Synthetic practice
text:
Recalculate Cell001 yourself
Cell001 has 663 mitochondrial counts out of 18,543 total counts:
[ 100=3.575473%. ]
Gene001 has raw count 125:
[ (1+10{,}000)=4.225532. ]
The following is R code. Open R from the project folder, run it, then exit with q(save = "no") before returning to terminal commands.
counts <- read.delim("data/synthetic/counts.tsv", check.names = FALSE)
genes <- read.delim("data/synthetic/gene-metadata.tsv")
x <- counts$Cell001
mito <- genes$is_mito[match(counts$gene_id, genes$gene_id)]
sum(x)
sum(x > 0)
100 * sum(x[mito]) / sum(x)
gene_count <- x[match("Gene001", counts$gene_id)]
log1p(10000 * gene_count / sum(x))
y <- readRDS("results/synthetic/normalized.rds")
y["Gene001", "Cell001"]
Compare the manual results with tables/cell-qc.tsv and the saved transformed value. Cell047 fails both depth and detected-gene cutoffs; Cell048 fails the mitochondrial cutoff.
crumbs: 10  Verify and Explain: Synthetic practice

title: Verify and Explain: Synthetic practice
text:
What the verifier establishes
It independently reads raw inputs and recalculates totals, detected genes, mitochondrial percentage and the QC decision. For a retained cell it checks the first positive gene’s transformed value. It does not call the workflow’s QC functions. It also rejects input files whose bytes changed after analysis. Even harmless TSV reformatting can therefore require a rerun.
This checks selected arithmetic and file consistency, not every matrix entry, PCA correctness or biological interpretation. It uses the cutoffs recorded with the results; a change to config/qc.tsv still requires you to rerun the workflow.
crumbs: 10  Verify and Explain: Synthetic practice

title: Verify and Explain: Synthetic practice
text:
Explain with limits
A defensible observation is: “Ten of 200 simulated cells fail the configured QC rules. Known simulated populations separate mainly along PC1, with variation within each population.” Add the actual variance percentages from your output. Do not call the separation statistically significant or claim biological cell-type discovery.
Your task: record a manual value, saved value and verdict for Cell001, then explain both exclusions in one sentence each. Name one aspect of the analysis that these checks do not verify.
Optional AI prompt: “Compare my calculation and interpretation with these exact saved values. Flag unsupported claims; do not invent a statistical test.”

title: Write: Synthetic practice
text:
Create a report you can defend
Open reports/synthetic-report.qmd. The helper creates a starter and a separate Quarto configuration for reports; it preserves an existing report. Replace the bracketed instructions with your own writing. Reports stay in the ignored reports/ folder, separate from the book.

title: Write: Synthetic practice
text: Rscript scripts/R/create_report.R synthetic

title: Write: Synthetic practice
text:
Build the result from evidence







Report section
Include




Question and data
The constructed-pattern question; 1,000 genes, 200 cells and two simulated populations


Methods
Input checks; 500 counts, 200 detected genes and 30% mitochondrial cutoffs; transformation and PCA choices


Results
190 retained cells; both QC figures/panels and the PCA observation


Verification
Cell001’s manual and saved values; reasons Cell047 and Cell048 were excluded


Limitations
Artificial sample labels, known simulation patterns and no biological inference



A concise worked paragraph is:

Of 200 simulated cells, 190 passed the configured QC rules. Cell001’s 18,543 total counts, 848 detected genes and 3.575473% mitochondrial fraction were independently checked. Gene001’s transformed expression was 4.225532. The two known simulated populations separated mainly along PC1; this demonstrates a constructed expression pattern rather than biological cell-type discovery.

Use this only after your own outputs agree. Add what PC1 and PC2 explain from results/synthetic/tables/pca-variance.tsv. Distinguish rounded display values from the full values used by the verifier.

title: Write: Synthetic practice
text:
Render and review
From the main project folder:
cd reports
quarto render synthetic-report.qmd
cd ..
Read reports/synthetic-report.html. Both figures should display; the HTML embeds them for sharing. Remove all bracketed starter text and confirm each number against its source table. If you already wrote a report before the folder changes, its image paths should point to ../results/synthetic/figures/.
Your task: identify one sentence supported by a calculation, one supported by a plot, and one stating a limitation. Record how you used AI and how you checked its contribution.
Before moving on: you can explain one retained cell, one exclusion and the limits of the PCA. Continue with Define: Zeisel mouse brain.

title: Define: Zeisel mouse brain
text:
The question
What variation in cell QC and expression is visible in a small subset of published mouse-brain cells after the same introductory workflow?
You now know the mechanics from synthetic practice. Real data add an important responsibility: understand where measurements and annotations came from before treating patterns as biological findings.
The example uses data from Zeisel and colleagues’ 2015 study, Cell types in the mouse cortex and hippocampus revealed by single-cell RNA-seq (paper). The R preparation script retrieves the dataset through scRNAseq::ZeiselBrainData() and exports the first 400 cells in source order from the main experiment.
This subset keeps a dense teaching analysis manageable. Source order is not a random or representative sampling scheme. Some published cell classes may be missing or overrepresented. We are not reproducing the full paper’s analysis or estimating tissue cell proportions.

title: Define: Zeisel mouse brain
text:
Set the scope before analysis
You can describe count depth, detected genes, mitochondrial fractions and exploratory PCA scores. You can check a published cell’s arithmetic. You cannot infer a treatment effect or donor-level difference because this guide has not validated donor/sample mapping. The teaching metadata explicitly use sample_id = unknown.
Published cell annotations are reference information. The workflow does not predict new identities, and its real-data PCA is not coloured by those labels.

title: Define: Zeisel mouse brain
text:
Your task
Write your descriptive question and a scope sentence:

This analysis describes the exported 400-cell subset; it does not estimate cell-type proportions or test a condition effect in the original study.

Then name two details to inspect in the source metadata before planning a broader analysis: for example, tissue region and the mapping of cells to animals or processing batches.
Optional AI prompt: “Critique this exploratory question using only the source and subset information I provide. What conclusions require validated donor or batch metadata?”
Before moving on: distinguish the published study, the downloaded source object and the 400-cell teaching subset.

title: Preview: Zeisel mouse brain
text:
Expect variation without assuming identities
The output names and calculations match synthetic practice. The inputs and interpretation change.
Run the example first, then return to these figures.

title: Preview: Zeisel mouse brain
text:
Output
What to inspect




results/zeisel/tables/cell-qc.tsv
Counts, detected genes, mitochondrial percentage and retention for every exported cell


results/zeisel/figures/qc.png
Broad variation in depth and whether either QC panel suggests a concern


results/zeisel/figures/pca.png
Expression variation among the retained cells


results/zeisel/tables/pca-variance.tsv
Fractions of selected-gene variance captured by PCs

title: Preview: Zeisel mouse brain
section: QC: passing is a specific decision
text:
QC: passing is a specific decision



QC for the 400-cell Zeisel teaching subset.


In the checked run, all 400 exported cells pass the illustrative cutoffs. Count totals and detected genes vary widely, and cells with greater count depth generally have more detected genes. The mitochondrial panel provides a separate check; the counts-versus-genes panel alone cannot reveal every QC concern.
“All pass these cutoffs” is a precise result. “All are high-quality cells” would claim more than these checks establish. The exported data are already a processed, published cell dataset, not raw droplets requiring cell calling.

title: Preview: Zeisel mouse brain
text:
PCA: structure needs explanation



Exploratory PCA of retained Zeisel cells.


Each point represents a retained cell. In the checked run, PC1 explains about 19.5% and PC2 about 9.9% of variation in the selected transformed genes. The plotted cells occupy separated regions and show variation within those regions. The axes together capture about 29.4%, not all expression variation.
The figure does not label those regions as cell types. Differences could reflect biology, count-related effects or other technical factors; this analysis does not separate those explanations. All points use the same colour deliberately.

title: Preview: Zeisel mouse brain
text:
Your task
Write one QC observation and one PCA observation using axis names and a saved number. Then add a limitation that follows from unvalidated donor mapping or the source-order subset. Do not name an apparent group from its position alone.
Before moving on: you know which outputs describe QC, which describe transformed expression, and why neither establishes a condition effect.

title: Meet: Zeisel mouse brain
text:
Retrieve and export the source
The first retrieval needs internet access and may download substantially more data than the 400 cells finally exported. The package can reuse its local data cache on later runs. The script exports the inputs again when rerun, so rerun Check, Run and Verify afterward rather than interpreting old results.
The retrieval call is scRNAseq::ZeiselBrainData(ensembl = FALSE, location = FALSE). The main assay contains UMI counts. Spike-ins and repeats are stored as alternative experiments and are not included in the teaching count matrix. The original featureType annotation identifies mitochondrial features. See the package documentation.

title: Meet: Zeisel mouse brain
text: Rscript scripts/R/prepare_zeisel.R

title: Meet: Zeisel mouse brain

Locate the evidence







File in data/zeisel/
Role




counts.rds
Sparse, gene-by-cell main-experiment count matrix


cell-metadata.tsv
Teaching cell IDs, unknown sample mapping and published labels


gene-metadata.tsv
Matching gene IDs and mitochondrial flags


source-cell-metadata.tsv
Original column metadata for the exported cells


source-gene-metadata.tsv
Original main-experiment feature metadata


provenance.txt, checksums.tsv
Retrieval settings, versions, selection and file checksums

title: Run: Zeisel mouse brain
text:
Follow the processing choices
The script:

Calculates raw totals, positive-count gene counts and mitochondrial percentages for every exported cell.
Retains cells passing all configured cutoffs.
Scales each retained cell to a total of 10,000 before applying log1p.
Selects up to 500 genes with highest positive variance in transformed expression.
Centers those genes and calculates PCA without unit-variance scaling.

It does not include published labels or sample IDs in these calculations. Mitochondrial features can still be selected for PCA. Different tissue composition or technical properties can therefore affect the displayed structure even after these QC rules.
This is a transparent introductory workflow. It does not resolve doublets, remove ambient RNA, correct batches or reproduce the complete published analysis. No hypothesis test or cell-type classifier is run.

Build a checked result paragraph
For the verified run, a starting point is:

The exported matrix contained 20,006 genes and 400 cells. All 400 passed the illustrative QC cutoffs. Cell 1772071015_C02 had 22,354 counts, 4,871 detected genes and a mitochondrial fraction of 3.462468%, confirmed by independent recalculation. Tshz1’s transformed value was 0.8510231. PCA showed expression structure within the convenience subset; this analysis did not establish cell identities or a condition effect.

text:
State limits and a useful follow-up
Do not translate “all passed QC” into a universal quality claim. Do not estimate tissue proportions or infer donor-level differences from this subset. A justified follow-up is to validate donor/tissue/batch mapping, inspect quality-related variation and design a fuller annotation or sample-level analysis before testing biological hypotheses.

title: Define: Your own study
text:
Start with an answerable descriptive question
Use this path after you can explain the synthetic and Zeisel examples. The goal is to adapt the workflow deliberately, not replace a dataset name and assume the interpretation transfers.
A suitable first question is:
Make it specific by naming the organism, tissue, count technology and collection context. If your intended question is “Does treatment change expression?”, this practical is only an exploratory starting point. Testing that question needs validated biological replication, confounder assessment and a suitable sample-level design.

title: Define: Your own study
text: After checking input structure and cell QC, what expression variation is visible among the retained cells in my study?

title: Define: Your own study
text:
Establish the units







Unit
What to record




Cell
A globally unique barcode/identifier


Sample
The biological specimen or preparation from which the cell came


Donor/animal
The independent biological source; one donor can contribute several samples


Condition
A measured treatment or study grouping, if available


Batch
Processing date, library or other technical grouping



Several thousand cells from one donor do not become several thousand independent donors. A source name, a library and a donor are not automatically interchangeable.

title: Define: Your own study
text:
Your task
Write a short analysis brief before preparing files:

State one descriptive question and why it matters.
Name the input source, organism, technology and count units.
State what is known about samples, donors, conditions and batches.
Name one conclusion the current inputs cannot support.

If mapping is genuinely unavailable, record it as unknown; do not infer it from a barcode without source documentation. A study lacking sufficient mapping can still support limited descriptive exploration, with that limitation stated.
Optional AI prompt: “Help me narrow this question using only the metadata I provide. List missing design information; do not fill it in or propose a condition test without replication.”
Before moving on: you have a written question, an explicit unit of observation and a boundary on interpretation.

title: Preview: Your own study
text:
Define success before seeing a pattern
A successful first run gives traceable QC decisions, exploratory expression outputs and an independently checked calculation. It does not guarantee separation, recognizable cell types or an interesting biological story.
Your own figures appear only after you supply inputs and run analysis. This page deliberately has no personal-study image placeholders.

Output inside results/your-study/
Your question




tables/cell-qc.tsv
Which cells were retained, and why?


figures/qc.png
How do depth, detected genes and mitochondrial fractions vary?


figures/pca.png
What structure is visible in this two-component projection?


tables/pca-variance.tsv
What fraction of selected-gene variation is shown?

Which cutoffs and input bytes produced the results?


normalized.rds, session-info.txt
Where are transformed values and software versions recorded?

title: Preview: Your own study
text:
Read observations cautiously
In QC, inspect both panels. Blue points pass all configured rules; red points fail at least one. Low counts and a high mitochondrial fraction are different reasons for exclusion. A threshold should be justified for your organism, tissue and technology, not copied because it worked for mouse brain.
In PCA, a point is a retained cell. Axes summarize variation in selected transformed expression, not treatment response or known cell identities. Distinct regions can motivate follow-up; overlap can also be a valid result. Do not change cutoffs simply to sharpen separation.
The own-study PCA uses a single point colour. Additional cell metadata are copied to the QC output but are not automatically used to colour PCA, adjust for batches or test a design.

title: Preview: Your own study
text:
Your task
Choose one output you will inspect first and explain why. Write two possible outcomes, including one without obvious separation, and what evidence you would need to interpret either.
Before moving on: you know which output supports each planned statement and are prepared to report an unremarkable result honestly.

title: Meet: Your own study
text:
Prepare three matching input files
Place your files in data/your-study/. This practical starts from a gene-count matrix with cells already identified, not FASTQ reads, alignments or an unfiltered droplet matrix.
Use tab-separated, UTF-8 text. Supply finite nonnegative integer counts. Do not use TPM, counts per 10,000 or log-transformed values as raw counts. Rounding normalized data does not recover raw counts.
Alternatively, save a matrix or Matrix object with row and column names as counts.rds. RDS takes precedence if both count files exist. Keep only the intended input representation so an old RDS cannot silently override a new TSV. This workflow converts counts to dense form and stops above 20 million entries; use an appropriate sparse workflow for larger studies.

title: Meet: Your own study
text:
File
Required structure




counts.tsv
First column gene_id; remaining columns unique cell IDs; genes in rows


cell-metadata.tsv
cell_id, sample_id, reference_label; one row per matrix cell


gene-metadata.tsv
gene_id, is_mito; one row per matrix gene

title: Meet: Your own study
text:
Annotate honestly
In cell metadata, sample_id must identify the originating sample where known. Use unassigned for an unavailable reference_label. Add donor, condition and batch columns when supported by documentation; the checker does not validate their biological meaning. If a sample mapping is genuinely unavailable, use unknown and restrict interpretation.
Use TRUE/FALSE mitochondrial flags from an organism- and identifier-matched annotation. Ensembl IDs should not be classified by assuming they start with MT-. The current input contract requires at least one flagged mitochondrial gene. If your organism or assay makes that metric inappropriate, pause and adapt the workflow explicitly rather than flagging an arbitrary gene to pass validation.
Metadata IDs must match matrix IDs exactly. Do not collapse duplicate gene symbols without documenting a valid aggregation rule. For merged libraries, ensure cell barcodes remain globally unique in both matrix and metadata.

title: Meet: Your own study
text:
Your task
Create a local source note recording data origin, acquisition date, preprocessing, count units, annotation version and any ID changes. Trace one cell and one gene across their files. Remove or protect participant-identifying fields before sharing data or AI prompts.
Before moving on: the file structure is documented and no missing annotation or sample information has been invented.

title: Check: Your own study
text:
Validate structure
Record the reported gene and cell counts and sample ID values. Compare them with what you expected from your source. A surprising count is a reason to inspect preparation, not merely a new fact to accept.
The script checks numeric raw counts, finite nonnegative integers, required columns, nonempty unique matrix/metadata IDs, exact matching sets and logical mitochondrial flags. It aligns metadata by ID. It does not validate donor assignment, gene annotation accuracy, participant consent, experimental design or batch/condition confounding.

title: Check: Your own study

Review the design manually
Confirm that cells map to the intended samples and that sample IDs have not been mistaken for donors. Inspect whether a condition occurs only in one processing batch or one donor. Extra metadata columns are retained for review; they do not become covariates in this introductory PCA.

title: Check: Your own study
text:
Choose and record QC cutoffs
Open config/qc.tsv. The your-study row initially contains 500 counts, 200 detected genes and 30% maximum mitochondrial counts. These are starting values in a teaching configuration, not validated criteria for your study.
Inspect source preprocessing and published assay guidance before deciding whether these are appropriate. A first documented run can show the distributions, but its retained set remains provisional until you review the QC panels. If you revise cutoffs, record the old and new values and rationale, then rerun Check, Run and Verify. Never choose cutoffs to manufacture PCA separation.
A cell passes only if all thresholds pass and its total is positive. The current workflow has no upper-count/doublet rule. High-count cells therefore need investigation even when they pass.

Optional AI prompt: “Review my input-check record and proposed QC criteria. Identify assumptions and missing evidence without inventing metadata or optimizing for a desired plot.”
Before moving on: file checks pass and any provisional choices or unresolved design limits are visible in your notes.

title: Run: Your own study

Generate the documented outputs
The script creates results/your-study/figures/ and results/your-study/tables/. It saves normalized.rds and session-info.txt directly in results/your-study/. Keep these distinct from raw inputs and learner reports.
If fewer than three cells pass QC, the script stops before PCA. Inspect the saved QC table and your source data; do not relax thresholds blindly. Successful completion means the requested calculations finished, not that your study design has been validated.

title: Run: Your own study
section: Understand what transfers from the examples
text:
Understand what transfers from the examples
The mathematics is unchanged: QC uses raw counts; retained cells are scaled to 10,000 before natural-log log1p; up to 500 positive-variance genes enter centered, unscaled PCA. Published labels and your added sample/donor columns are not used to adjust the PCA. Mitochondrial genes remain eligible for selection.
Normalization changes numerical scale. It does not restore missing measurements, prove biological comparability or remove all technical effects. This script does not fit a treatment model, resolve doublets, correct batches or infer cell types.

title: Run: Your own study
text:
Inspect before interpreting
Read tables/cell-qc.tsv, then view both QC panels. If sample IDs are available, compare retained counts by sample rather than relying only on an overall percentage. For example, this is R-console code:
qc <- read.delim("results/your-study/tables/cell-qc.tsv")
with(qc, table(sample_id, retained))
Exit R before using terminal commands again. Disproportionate loss from one sample can affect later comparisons and deserves investigation.
Next inspect PCA and tables/pca-variance.tsv. Multiply fractions by 100 for axis percentages. A clear visual pattern is a question to investigate; it is not an automatically identified cell type or a significant difference.

Turn notes into a defensible account







Section

Source, organism, assay, raw-count units, samples/donors and known design limits

title: Appendix A — Appendix
text:
Installation troubleshooting
Stop at the first failed command. Read the first error, not only the final snapshot or dependency error. Keep your existing lockfile; do not snapshot an incomplete installation or switch repositories to chase a missing dependency.

title: Appendix A — Appendix
text:
Mac: library 'ssl' not found
This is a missing system library used while compiling some package dependencies. It is different from the R package named openssl. Use this targeted fix only if you see that compiler error.
Exit R with q(save = "no"). In the terminal, install the library using the official R-for-macOS helper:
sudo Rscript --vanilla -e 'source("https://mac.R-project.org/bin/install.R"); install.libs("openssl")'
Enter your Mac login password; typing is invisible. This administrator command installs system libraries. Run project setup and package installation as your normal user.
On Apple Silicon, check:
ls -l /opt/R/arm64/lib/libssl* /opt/R/arm64/lib/libcrypto*
After a successful installation, rerun Rscript scripts/R/setup.R from the main project folder. Do not continue if permission errors remain. Other architectures use different library paths; consult the official macOS library instructions.


Source compilation and missing binaries
Binary packages may not be available for every package/R combination. The supplied lockfile can therefore require source compilation. On macOS, install Apple’s Command Line Tools if the error says the compiler is missing:
xcode-select --install
Follow the installer, then rerun setup. Other missing system dependencies require their own remedy; the OpenSSL command is not a general fix. If an error remains, share the first compiler error, R version and operating system with the maintainer.


Missing packages or an out-of-sync environment
Run in the terminal:
Rscript -e 'renv::status()'
The project’s default snapshot type is all, matching its lockfile. Learners should restore through setup, not regenerate the lockfile. If restoration completes but status still reports inconsistent packages, share the full status output with the maintainer. A message that CRAN repositories replace defaults does not itself establish that installation failed; inspect subsequent errors.

title: Appendix A — Appendix
text:
Workflow troubleshooting







Symptom
What to check




Rscript entered at an R > prompt
Exit R using q(save = "no"); use the terminal.


Missing input file
Open the main project folder and run the example’s preparation step.


Missing matrix dimensions
Use the current scripts; they load Matrix before reading sparse RDS counts.


Duplicate or mismatched IDs
Correct the input metadata; matching by order alone is insufficient.


No cells retained
Inspect QC cutoffs and source preprocessing before changing thresholds.


Verification says input files changed
Rerun Check, Run and Verify using the current input files.


Old metrics after changing synthetic data
Recreate v2 inputs and rerun analysis; old 48-cell values do not apply.


Missing plot in the book or report
Run that dataset’s workflow; plots belong in results/DATASET/figures/.


Missing QC table
Rerun the current workflow; all TSV outputs belong in results/DATASET/tables/.


null device followed by 1
Normal output after R finishes writing a plot.



Old plots and TSV tables directly inside a dataset’s results folder are obsolete after migration. Only remove them after a successful rerun and verification. Keep normalized.rds and session-info.txt directly in that folder. Learner report writing stays in ignored reports/.

title: Appendix A — Appendix
text:
Methods and boundaries
This practical introduces QC, normalization and PCA. It does not perform droplet calling, clustering, automated cell labeling, UMAP, differential expression, integration or pseudobulk testing. Extend the analysis only after learners can defend input choices, QC and normalization. Cells from one donor are not independent biological replicates.
PCA signs can flip across numerical implementations without changing the geometry. Compare variance explained and relative geometry rather than insisting on identical PC signs. Reproducibility requires the same input bytes, gene annotation, R and packages; retain checksums and session information.
The Zeisel example uses the first 400 source-order cells and has unvalidated donor mapping. Its proportions and apparent groups cannot be generalized to the full tissue. Published labels are context, not predictions made by this workflow.

title: Appendix A — Appendix
text:
Sources

Zeisel et al. 2015.
scRNAseq documentation.
Single-cell analysis with Bioconductor.
renv introduction.
R-for-macOS system libraries.
Quarto books.

title: Appendix A — Appendix
text:
Terms used in the practical







Term
Meaning in this workflow




Total counts
Sum over all genes in the input main-experiment matrix for one cell


Detected genes
Number of genes with count greater than zero in a cell


Mitochondrial percentage
Fraction of that cell’s counts assigned to flagged mitochondrial genes, multiplied by 100


Retained cell
A cell passing all configured QC rules; this is not a universal quality guarantee


Counts per 10,000
Raw counts divided by the cell total and multiplied by 10,000 before logging


log1p
Natural logarithm of one plus a value


PCA score
A cell’s coordinate on a component calculated from selected transformed genes


Reference label
An existing annotation or known simulation setting; not a prediction made here


Input checksum
A fingerprint used to detect changed file bytes, not a validation of biological correctness

title: Appendix A — Appendix
text:
Read beyond the introductory workflow
The OSCA QC chapter discusses QC choices for single-cell data. The OSCA normalization chapter explains scaling and more detailed normalization approaches. This practical uses its own explicitly documented cutoffs and counts-per-10,000 transformation; it is not an implementation of every OSCA procedure.
For a subsequent biological study, plan the design and metadata review before adding a cell-type classifier, batch correction or a condition test. Those methods answer additional questions and introduce assumptions that the current QC/PCA script does not evaluate.
